# Transcaval Access for Large-Bore Structural Heart Interventions: A Clinical Review

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore structural heart interventions have revolutionized cardiovascular medicine. However, severe aortoiliac disease, calcification, and tortuosity frequently preclude conventional transfemoral access [1]. While surgical alternative access sites—including transapical [2], transaortic [3,4], transsubclavian/axillary [5], and transcarotid [6]—have been developed, they often require general anesthesia and are associated with significant surgical morbidity [7,8]. To address these limitations, transcaval access emerged as a completely percutaneous alternative, utilizing the venous system to cross directly into the abdominal aorta [1,9].

Careful pre-procedural planning is the cornerstone of a successful transcaval procedure. High-resolution multidetector computed tomography (CT) imaging is utilized to identify a suitable "crossing window" where the abdominal aorta and the inferior vena cava (IVC) are adjacent, free of interposed bowel, major vessel branches, or severe calcification [10,11,12].

The procedure is performed in a catheterization laboratory under fluoroscopic guidance. From a right femoral vein access, a catheter is positioned in the IVC opposite the target abdominal aorta site. From the femoral artery, a target snare or catheter is placed in the aorta. Utilizing electrosurgical energy—typically a standard coronary guidewire electrified with a radiofrequency generator—the operator punctures the wall of the IVC, crosses the retroperitoneal space, and enters the abdominal aorta, trapping the wire inside the aortic target [13,14]. Once secure wire position is established, the tract is dilated with a standard balloon, and a large-bore sheath is introduced directly into the aorta [9,13].

Following completion of the structural heart intervention, the aortic puncture site is closed using a nitinol mesh closure device, most commonly the Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO I or II) [15,16]. Because the retroperitoneal pressure is lower than the intravascular pressure, the venous side acts as a safety valve, directing residual aortic bleeding directly into the IVC rather than the retroperitoneum, which significantly mitigates the risk of catastrophic retroperitoneal hemorrhage [17,18].

The prospective, multicenter National Institutes of Health (NIH) transcaval study enrolled 100 high-risk patients ineligible for standard transfemoral TAVR, demonstrating a 99% successful transcaval access rate and a 30-day survival rate of 92%, confirming the clinical viability of the technique [18]. Subsequent large registries, such as the Transcaval TAVR Registry, have validated these findings in broader real-world cohorts, demonstrating high procedural success rates comparable to or exceeding other alternative access routes [19,20]. Comparative studies have shown that transcaval access is associated with shorter hospital stays and fewer major adverse events than surgical transapical or transaortic access [7,8,21,22,23]. However, like any advanced technique, transcaval access is associated with a distinct learning curve [24]. Multicenter studies indicate that procedural time and complication rates decline significantly after an operator's first 10 to 15 cases [24].

Although initially developed for TAVR, the utility of transcaval access has expanded to other large-bore endovascular interventions. It has been successfully utilized for thoracic and abdominal endovascular aneurysm repair (TEVAR/EVAR) in patients with hostile iliofemoral anatomy [25,26,27]. Additionally, transcaval access has emerged as a crucial portal for mechanical circulatory support (MCS). In cardiogenic shock, high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention, or failing ventricles, transcaval access allows the percutaneous insertion of large-bore MCS devices, such as the Impella 5.0 or 5.5, which would otherwise require surgical cutdown [28,29].

Despite its safety profile, transcaval access is not without risks. Major vascular complications, including retroperitoneal hematoma, aortic dissection, or closure device embolization, can occur but are relatively rare [19,22]. The most common unique sequela is a persistent aortocaval arteriovenous fistula (AVF) [30]. While most of these fistulas are hemodynamically insignificant and close spontaneously over several months, a minority may persist, requiring secondary percutaneous intervention or closure device adjustments [30]. Long-term follow-up from clinical trials indicates that the vast majority of AVFs resolve without adverse clinical sequelae [18].

In conclusion, transcaval access represents a highly effective, completely percutaneous alternative for patients requiring large-bore structural heart or endovascular interventions who lack viable transfemoral options. Ongoing innovations in dedicated closure devices and refined crossing systems are expected to further simplify the procedure, reduce complications, and solidify its role in the modern heart team's armamentarium.
